physical_harm: Injuries including cut injury on chin, bruise marks on neck and back, fractured trachea, and death due to asphyxia from throttling
number_of_offences: Two offences charged (rape and murder), both upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The version of the eye-witness (PW-1) is reliable and the same is corroborated by evidence of another witness (PW-2) and also by medical evidence.
witness_credibility: The trial court and the High Court rightly held that there was no reason to disbelieve the version of PW-1 (the eye-witness) and the corroborative evidence of PW-2, (father of the deceased).
trial_duration: Offence: 29.03.2000; Trial judgment: 18.03.2006; High Court decision: 26.09.2006; Supreme Court decision: 03.05.2013
legal_representation: Pandit Parmanand Katara, Abhishek Sharma, C.K. Sucharita, Kusum Lata Sharma for the Appellant; Navnit Kumar, Avijit Roy, Corporate Law Group for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced; High Court: Confirmed conviction, reduced death sentence to life imprisonment and life imprisonment to 7 years imprisonment; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal, upheld High Court's decision
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the version of the eye-witness PW-1 is reliable and corroborated by evidence of another witness PW-2 and medical evidence. The evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 9 as well as the statement of co-villagers supports the prosecution story.
defence_argument: The accused contended that conviction could not have been based upon sole testimony of PW-1 as the same is not reliable. Also, the doctor's remarks that no mark of sexual violence was found on the genital organs of the deceased made the conviction under Section 376 unsustainable. The accused also argued that after the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment, he should have been released after expiry of 14 years.
legal_principle_applied: Life imprisonment means imprisonment for whole of life subject to the remission power granted under Articles 72 and 161 of the Constitution of India. When death sentence is commuted to life imprisonment, the executive power of remission to be exercised cautiously, taking note of the gravity of the offence.
precedent_relied_upon: Life Convict @ Khoka Prasanta Sen vs. B.K. Srivastava and Ors. (2013) 3 SCC 425; Mohinder Singh vs. State of Punjab (2013) 3 SCC 294; Sangeet and Anr. vs. State of Haryana (2013) 2 SCC 452; Rameshbhai Chandubhai B Rathod (2) vs. State of Gujarat (2011) 2 SCC 764; Chhote Lal vs. State of Madhya Pradesh (2011) 8 SCR 239; Mui/a and Anr. vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010) 3 SCC 508; Maru Ram vs. Union of India and Ors. (1981) 1 SCC 107; State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Ratan Singh and Ors. (1976) 3 SCC 470; Gopal Vinayak Godse vs. State of Maharashtra AIR 1961 SC 600; Swami Shraddananda (2) @ Murli Manohar Mishra vs. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Sahib Hussain @ Sahib Jan vs. State of Rajasthan 2013 (6) Scale 219
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the heinous nature of the crime, which involved rape and murder, and the fact that the accused threw the dead body in a place surrounded by bushes and shrubs. The High Court considered that the case did not come under the 'rarest of rare' category and therefore reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court weighed the accused's age (33 years) and the fact that the case did not come under the 'rarest of rare' category as mitigating factors.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the heinous nature of the crime, including rape and murder, and the act of throwing the dead body in a place surrounded by bushes and shrubs as aggravating factors.
